overview: Samori Ture built a state through conquest, trade and Islamic authority in the later 1800s. Often called the Wassoulou or Samorian empire, it shifted eastward under French military pressure. “First” and “Second Samori Empire” describe different territorial phases of the same ruler’s state. Its independent history ended with his capture in 1898, not with the 1900 to 1914 interval currently attached to those two map labels.

periods.title: Building a western state
periods.summary: From an early 1860s base, Samori expanded and established himself at Bissandougou.

periods.title: Migration and an eastern state
periods.summary: Samori moved his forces and many followers east, seeking territory and supply routes while continuing to resist France.

periods.title: After capture
periods.summary: The state lost independent power in 1898. Any map coverage after this belongs to the atlas’s unresolved chronology, not a revived Samorian empire.

sections.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation

items.text: Samori’s armies depended on supply networks. Earlier muskets came chiefly through Freetown, while horses came from the northwestern Sudan. These routes connected inland politics with coastal commerce.

In 1891 to 1892, negotiations with Freetown traders brought breechloading and repeating firearms. Legassick also records a local firearms industry established by this period. Adaptation meant acquiring weapons and developing skilled work to support them.

After French advances restricted western supplies, Samori sought weapons through the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast and horses through Mossi country. Existing African trade routes became crucial to the state’s survival.
The Buré goldfields mattered to Samori’s economy. When French forces occupied Buré in 1885, his armies drove them back. Control of a resource region could be as consequential as control of a capital.

sections.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire

items.text: Samori sought an agreement with the British authorities in Sierra Leone and also negotiated treaties with France. His strategy combined fighting and bargaining; African rulers were participants in diplomacy, not merely spectators to European decisions.

Trade also carried a terrible cost: Samori captured and sold people to help finance guns and horses. Resistance to French conquest did not mean freedom for everyone living under his own expanding power.

Yves Person’s chronology records a decision in 1892 to move east with a substantial part of the population. A moving state meant uprooted households as well as marching soldiers. The chronology establishes the displacement without telling us every family’s experience.

The same chronology records scorched-earth tactics in 1891. Destroying resources could obstruct an advancing army while making civilian life more precarious. Military success and the welfare of local people cannot be treated as the same thing.

sections.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain

items.text: Sordi’s fortified settlement in northern Côte d’Ivoire became part of the struggle between Kénédougou, Samori’s forces and French expansion. Historian M’Brah identifies occupation by Samori’s sofa troops from 1896 to 1898. A single site reveals overlapping rulers and local experiences.

M’Brah traces Diawala’s growth to people dispersed from Sordi and to exiles returning after Kénédougou’s defeat in 1898. Related families reunited and organized a new settlement. Political defeat changed where people lived; it did not erase their family connections.

Accounts of Samori need careful comparison. Legassick’s article explicitly warns that some French visitors’ descriptions were imaginative or unreliable. Historians use local traditions and archival evidence together instead of treating an officer’s vivid story as automatic fact.

This dossier has not verified a short original-script passage from a securely identified Samorian document. Arabic scholarship belonged to the wider region, but substituting an unrelated manuscript would give a false impression. Household sanitation and specific medical routines also remain unestablished by the sources used here.

French forces captured Samori on 29 September 1898. He was exiled to Gabon and died in 1900. His death date is therefore not the date a “first” or “second” empire began; those map labels need chronological correction.

ending.text: Samori’s capture by French forces in 1898 ended his independent state. Exile and his death in 1900 followed. The region’s communities continued under colonial rule; the changing imperial labels describe political power, not the appearance or disappearance of a people.
